message.description: Your full report for your caller

attachment.cliPrefix: You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude, running within the Claude Agent SDK.

content.content:
1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
120

1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
21	- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
22	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
23	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
24	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
25	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
26	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
27	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
28	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
29	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
30	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
31	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
32	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
33	
34	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
35	
36	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
37	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
38	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
39	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
40	5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
41	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
42	
43	In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
44	
45	- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
46	- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
47	- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
48	- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
49	- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
50	- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
51	
52	An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
53	
54	- keep: every check passes;
55	- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
56	- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
57	- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.
58	
59	Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
60	
61	## Reading and writing
62	
63	- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
64	- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
65	- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
66	- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
67	- Commit the record file and its history together.
68	- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
69	- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.
70	
71	## The pass
72	
73	Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.
74	
75	The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.
76	
77	1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
78	2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
79	3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
80	   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
81	   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
82	   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
83	4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
84	5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.
85	
86	Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.
87	
88	## A consolidation
89	
90	A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").
91	
92	- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
93	- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
94	- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
95	- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
96	- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
97	- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
98	- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.
99	
100	## The consolidation tools
101	
102	Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Put the open questions of the runs on the review queue.
103	
104	Pick the tool by the job:
105	
106	- To bring the record in line with a landing: the record-landing workflow (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`.
107	- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
108	- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
109	- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
110	- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.
111	
112	## INDEX and the gap ledger
113	
114	- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
115	- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
116	- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
117	- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
118	- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.
119

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
51	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
52

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

45	## 3. What could not be matched, and what was chosen
46	
47	**The order of the sums longer than 16 terms, and only that.** Everything else the Java computes by the operations of the Fortress source in its order: a division stays a division (no reciprocal), no fused multiply-add, the masked attention entries and the padded rows are computed as the Fortress computes them, `10.0^(-5)` is the folded constant `1e-5` and `beta1^t` is `Math.pow`, as walk's native is (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java:76-78`).
48	
49	- The library's matrix product adds the terms of each element in ascending order of the summed index: `Matrix.mul` splits the summed dimension in sequence, and forks only the rows and the columns (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`). The Java's products add in the same order. Only the first term differs in form (the library stores it, the Java adds it to 0.0), which cannot change a value other than the sign of a zero.
50	- The library's `DOT`, `SUM` and `BIG MAX` are reductions over a range. A range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements splits at a power-of-two boundary and joins the two results (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`, `:1310-1327`); at most 16 elements fold left to right from the identity (`:1365-1373`). In the model at batch 1 the only sums of more than 16 terms are the softmax over the 27 logits (`sm` on line 61), which the library adds as (16 terms) + (11 terms). The Java adds all 27 left to right. That is the last-digit difference from walk above. The fork/join variant of section 6 adds them as the library does.
51	- With more than one document in a batch, `SUM vm` and the loss's `DOT` are also longer than 16.
52	
53	**The parser is ported, not replaced.** `FlatData.parseFloat` accumulates the mantissa digit by digit in a double and scales once, so it is not correctly rounded. `./run.sh parse`:
54	
55	    4192 numbers, 699 differ from Double.parseDouble, the worst by 2.0 ulp
56	
57	So 699 of the 4,192 initial parameters that the flat program trains from are not the doubles nearest to the decimal text of the weight files. The Java uses the same arithmetic, so that it starts from the same parameters; with `Double.parseDouble` it would start from other ones. The loader check passes at tolerance 0 either way, because it reads `P0.txt` through the same parser.
58	
59	**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers these; each says which reading was acted on.
60	
61	1. *Same operations per element, sums left to right.* The alternative, reordering sums or replacing divisions where the tolerance holds, would be faster in places (section 5) and was not taken in the baseline, so that a ratio of compiled Fortress to this program measures the implementation and not a different arithmetic. The Vector API variant shows what one reordering buys.
62	2. *Dense, as the Fortress.* All 16 positions of every document are computed, and all 16 by 16 attention entries, also those that the mask sends to exactly 0. Skipping them is an algorithmic saving open to both programs alike.
63	3. *Storage reused.* One step's arrays are allocated once per batch size and reused, and `adam` updates `p`, `m` and `v` in place, where the Fortress makes new arrays and returns three new vectors. What this saves was not measured.
64	4. *Products read the weights in place.* `x w^T` is a dot product of two rows. A version that copied each transposed weight matrix first, so that the inner loop ran along rows of both operands, measured the same within noise in one fork (step 109 against 101 microseconds, taken at different loads) and was dropped.
65	5. *No lambdas.* The row bodies are anonymous classes. With lambdas the first step of a cold JVM took 30 ms instead of 5 ms (one run each), the cost of the first lambda's bootstrap.
66	6. *The model reaches loops and sums through four seams* (`forRange`, `dot`, `sum`, `max` in `FlatArrays`), so that the two variants replace the vocabulary alone. After warm-up the step measured the same with and without the seams (101.9 against 100.9 and 102.5 microseconds, one or two forks each).

195	## 6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime
196	
197	`variants/forkjoin/FlatArrays.java` gives the vocabulary's loops and sums the shape that the Fortress library and its compiled runtime give parallel work, on a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`. What a piece computes once it is no longer split is the baseline's plain loop, so its time is a floor for what compiled Fortress could reach with this structure and unboxed arrays.

201	| a parallel range | `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1310-1345`: a range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements (`:20`) splits at the highest power-of-two boundary inside it; the two parts are the arms of a `do ... also do` | `forRange`, used by the model's row loops (`rows(rmsn)`, `rows(sm)`, ...), by `adam`'s loop over the 4,192 elements, by the loop over the planes and by the elementwise passes |
202	| a reduction | the same split, the two results joined; at most 16 elements fold left to right (`:1365-1373`) | `dot`, `sum`, `max`: no shared accumulator |

302	## 8. The lines of the Fortress that were hardest to read as an algorithm
303	
304	- `MicroGptFlat.fss:59`, `a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)`. Three things on it are not visible from the line: the juxtaposition of two rank-3 arrays is a product on every pair of planes (`FlatArrays.fss:127`), `^T` on a rank-3 array transposes every plane (`MicroGptFlat.fss:24`), and `mask +` adds one matrix to every plane (`FlatArrays.fss:135`). Every operand has the type `Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]`, so no shape is on the page; the shapes had to be worked out from `heads` (`FlatArrays.fss:84-96`), whose index arithmetic `(q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j` is itself juxtaposition for multiplication between integer names.
305	- `MicroGptFlat.fss:66`, `dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)`: which of the four `rows` it is (the one over two rank-3 arrays), and that `dh vh^T` groups as `dh (vh^T)`.
306	- `MicroGptFlat.fss:63`, `diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize))`: a juxtaposition of a diagonal object and a matrix that scales the rows; `MicroGptFlat.fss:70`, a scatter-add written as a product with a transposed 0/1 matrix.
307	- `MicroGptFlat.fss:32`, `(dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r`: `y (...)` reads as an application and is a scaling; `|y|` is the number of elements, not a norm.
308	- The order in which a sum is added is on no line of the model. It took the library's `Matrix.mul`, `Vector.dot` and the range's `generate` to learn that a product adds in sequence and a dot product over more than 16 elements does not.
309	- `MicroGptFlat.fss:18`, `10.0^(-5)`: whether it is `Math.pow` at run time or a folded constant decides the last bit of `epsilon`; the skill's rule on numerals settles it (folded).

All five lines were measured on 2026-11-10 between 14:36 and 14:46 UTC on this machine, one program after another, with another worker's builds and runs beside them (load 1.6 to 5.4 on 4 CPUs). Section 4 gives the method and the spread.

21	- dzaima flat / Java = 115; dzaima flat / NumPy = 65.
22	- pure Python / Java = 1,180 as each program runs. The pure Python program does less work in a step: it computes only the document's positions, 7.3 on average, where the flat programs compute 16. Per position, pure Python takes 18.2 ms and Java 0.0070 ms: 2,600 times.

25	Which comparisons are of one session: all of them. The Python, NumPy and dzaima runs were interleaved in five rounds, and the Java bench ran between rounds 3 and 4. The Java number is from the Java worker's program as it stood uncommitted at 14:42; `java-baseline/REPORT.md` did not exist when this note was written, after 24 minutes of polling, so the Java worker's own timings are not compared here, and the program may have changed since (section 4, "Java").
26	
27	**His expectation.** "Java faster than pure Python": holds, by three orders of magnitude. "Java slower than NumPy": does not hold at this size. Java is 1.8 times faster at batch 1, and about level at batch 4 (Java 404 µs, NumPy 414 µs for the step alone).
28	
29	**The reason, by reading.** At widths of 16 the step is about 200,000 multiply-adds: the forward products are about 64,000 (three 16×16 by 16×16 for Q, K, V; 4 heads of 16×4 by 4×16 and 16×16 by 16×4; one 16×16; two between 16 and 64 wide; one to 27 wide), and each has two products in the backward pass.
30	
31	- *Java* does that arithmetic and little else. 0.113 ms for 200,000 multiply-adds is about 1.8 billion a second, the rate of scalar double arithmetic on one core of this machine. Its step is bound by arithmetic.
32	- *NumPy* makes 190 function calls per step, counted by `cProfile`, 29 of them matrix products. On this machine a 16×16 by 16×16 product costs 0.80 µs, `x*x` on 16×16 0.33 µs, `np.sqrt` 0.46 µs, and a `mean(-1, keepdims=True)` 2.3 µs; the arithmetic inside a 16×16 product is 4,096 multiply-adds, about 1 µs of scalar work and less in BLAS. So each call pays as much for the interpreter, argument checking, dispatch and the result's allocation as for its arithmetic: 190 calls at about 1 µs is the 0.2 ms. NumPy's step is bound by the number of calls, not by the arithmetic, and BLAS has nothing to win on 16×16. The same is in the record from a third party: at this size a GPU under PyTorch loses to NumPy because launch overhead dominates 16×16 products (`apl/reference/nydhal-dyalog/README.md:193-196`).
33	- *Pure Python* builds a graph of scalar `Value` objects: 59,647 nodes for a document of 7 positions, about 8,300 per position, counted in the program. Each node is an object allocation, a tuple of children and a tuple of local gradients in the forward pass, then a visit in the topological sort and a loop over children in the backward pass; Adam is a Python loop over 4,192 objects. 120 ms for 60,000 nodes is 2 µs a node. Its step is bound by interpreted bytecode and allocation per scalar operation.
34	- *dzaima/APL* interprets a tree in Java. Its matrix product in these programs is a dfn, `mm←{↑(↓⍺)∘.{+/⍺×⍵}↓⍉⍵}`, which calls an interpreted function once per element of the result: about 4,000 calls in the forward pass and twice that in the backward. Its step is bound by interpreted calls per element, which is why it sits between pure Python (interpreted per scalar operation) and NumPy (interpreted per array operation).
35	
36	His expectation is the usual result for larger arrays, where the BLAS kernel outruns a plain Java loop. This model is below that size. In this session NumPy's step alone went from 0.17–0.24 ms at batch 1 to 0.41 ms at batch 4, 1.41 ms at batch 16 and 2.66 ms at batch 32, about 83 µs a document at batch 32; Java's went from 0.101 ms at batch 1 to 0.404 ms at batch 4, 101 µs a document. So NumPy passes Java somewhere above batch 4, by a small factor. These batch timings were taken under load 3.5 to 4.7, with OpenBLAS's thread count left at its default, and the Java bench has no batch above 4, so the crossing is not measured.

125	## 6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler
126	
127	To see whether the second set disturbed the first, the five prelude jars of this tree were compared with the base build's, class by class, after the tree's path was rewritten in each class's constants.
128	
129	    base build's jars against the base build's code, compiled again cold:        590 classes, 590 equal
130	    base build's jars against the base build's code over this tree's sources:    590 equal
131	    base build's jars against this tree's jars:                                  558 equal, 32 differ
132	    this tree's CompilerBuiltin, compiled twice:                                 312 classes, 16 differ
133	    the base build's code with -XX:hashCode=0, and with =1:                      312 classes, 18 differ each
134	
135	The classes that differ hold the same methods in another order, and their dispatch methods test the same types in another order (`javap` of `CompilerBuiltin$EqualTo` and `CompilerBuiltin`). So the order in which the code generator writes methods and dispatch tests follows the JVM's identity hashes. The base's code gives the same bytes on each compile only because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run; a changed hash mode moves the order, and this tree's code gives a different order on each compile. Which of the tree's edits unsettles it was not traced. The rehearsal saw the same for the one library ("Which copy comes first is not stable from one compile to the next", its W6).
136	
137	For probe Y it means that a comparison of bytes cannot show that the prelude is undisturbed; the tests have to. For the work it means that a compiled test can pass or fail with the order (the rehearsal's W6 was such a case), and that no two builds of different code give comparable jars.

3	# Which class carries a built-in type on the compiled path: the ways
4	
5	## The answer in short
6	
7	- A carrier is the JVM class whose instances are the values of a built-in type at run time. Today `FZZ32`, a class written by hand in Java, carries the prelude's `ZZ32`.
8	- The two libraries declare a built-in type in two shapes. The prelude says `trait ZZ32`, and `FZZ32` is the trait's class. The interpreter's library says `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, and `value object Boolean` with no trait at all.
9	- I found nine ways. Four give the type its class (A to D). Three are ruled out (E, F, G). Two are later layers for speed, not carriers (H, I).
10	- The four that count:
11	  - **A.** The trait's class is written by hand, and the objects leave the library. This is the prelude's way, whole.
12	  - **B.** The trait's class is written by hand, and an empty object stands below each trait. This is the rehearsal's hack.
13	  - **C.** The object's class carries the value. The trait stays a plain interface. The library's text does not change. This is walk's own way, brought to the compiled path.
14	  - **D.** One object per type: each number trait is merged with its one object, as `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char` already are. Then C's machinery, with one name per type.
15	- The team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, and the peers do not point to one way. The library as written points to C. The peers point to D. The team's later code is A's shape, but its author called it a special case "for the time being", and its own plan for unboxing is written over objects and `comprises` clauses, which is C's and D's shape.
16	- I recommend C now, and D as a second step that the curator rules on apart. C changes no line of the library, keeps walk as it is, removes W13 and W14 by construction, and closes the hole of ledger row 866. It gives up the prelude's trick of one hand-written class per type with no change in the code generator: the code generator must learn that a native object has a payload.
17	
18	## The words
19	
20	- **Built-in type.** A type whose values the language's implementation makes, not a constructor call: the numbers, `Boolean`, `Char`, the flat string, and a few Java-backed values (a reader, a writer, an array's store).
21	- **Carrier.** The JVM class of a built-in type's values on the compiled path.
22	- **Payload.** The Java value inside a carrier: an `int` in `FZZ32`, a `double` in `FRR64`, a `java.lang.String` in `FJavaString`.
23	- **Box.** A carrier object on the heap. A number is unboxed where the compiled code holds the payload itself: a JVM `double` in a local, a field or an array.
24	- **Springboard.** The class `T$DefaultTraitMethods` that the code generator writes for a trait `T`. It holds the trait's method bodies. An object's class extends the springboard of the first trait that the object extends (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:888-909`).
25	- **Stub.** A Java source file that declares, empty, the classes that the code generator will write, so that hand-written Java can extend them before any Fortress is compiled: `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`.
26	- **Closed type.** A type that no program can extend: an object, or a trait whose `comprises` clause lists its only subtypes. An open type is a trait without such a clause.
27	- **Native component.** A component declared `native component`. The specification says that inside one "the syntax and semantics are implementation dependent" (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:513-518`). The library's four are `FortressBuiltin`, `FlatString`, `Reflect` and `AnyType`.

375	## The peers
376	
377	Context only.
378	
379	- **Scala.** `Int` is declared `final abstract class Int extends AnyVal`: one final type, no interface above it. The compiler maps it to a JVM `int` and boxes it to `java.lang.Integer` where it meets `Any` or a type parameter. A value class (`class Meter(val v: Double) extends AnyVal`) is a one-field wrapper that the compiler erases to its field.
380	- **Kotlin.** `Int` is a final class of the standard library with intrinsic members. It is a JVM `int` where it is not nullable and not a type argument, and a `java.lang.Integer` elsewhere. `@JvmInline value class` is the one-field wrapper.
381	- **Swift.** `struct Int { var _value: Builtin.Int64 }` in the standard library: a struct over a compiler's builtin type, with its operators written in the library over builtin operations, and protocols joined by extension. This is way E with a real bottom type, which Fortress lacks.
382	- **Julia.** `primitive type Int64 <: Signed 64 end`: a concrete, final leaf below abstract types (`Signed`, `Integer`, `Real`, `Number`). Only an abstract type can have subtypes. Arrays of such leaves are stored inline, and code is specialised for each concrete type.
383	
384	All four make the built-in type itself one final, concrete type: way D's shape. Julia's abstract types above a final leaf are way C's and D's shape for `Number` and `AnyIntegral`. None has a second name for the same values. Scala and Kotlin show way H over it.
